evidence: Verg. G. 2.154: in spīram tractū sē colligit anguis
Cato Agr. 77: spīram sīc facitō, a coiled cake
terms.comment: Greek σπεῖρα: anything wound round on itself, a snake’s coil, a coil of rope, a twisted cake, the base of a column (Lewis & Short). For a spiral drawn on paper it is the nearest classical noun; “in a spiral” is in spīram.

terms.gloss: spirally, wound like a snail’s shell
terms.comment: Adverbial phrase: “in the form of a snail”. Lewis & Short spells the word coclea or cochlea; the lexicon writes cochlea (see “snail”).

terms.gloss: a volute, a spiral scroll on a column’s capital

phrases.latin: Cochleae testam spectā: in spīram torta est.
phrases.english: Look at the snail’s shell: it’s twisted into a spiral.

phrases.latin: Ā mediō incipe et circumage manum: spīram facis.
phrases.english: Start from the middle and go round and round with your hand: you’re making a spiral.

phrases.latin: neque tantō squāmeus in spīram tractū sē colligit anguis
phrases.english: nor does the scaly snake gather itself into so vast a coil

sources: Lewis & Short: spira · Lewis & Short: coclea · Lewis & Short: voluta
